pending_articles.title: Sentence-level neural dynamics in speech motor cortex
pending_articles.content: Prior recordings from speech motor cortex have revealed phonemic, syllabic, articulatory and speech-sequence representations, while more recent studies indicate that activity may also reflect higher-order features of speech production. However, whether speech motor cortex is sensitive to the linguistic organization of sentences remains unclear. Here we show that single-unit activity in speech motor cortex contains information about sentence-level linguistic structure. In three BrainGate2 participants with implanted microelectrode arrays in the left precentral gyrus, we recorded neural activity during an instructed-delay speech task comprising English sentences, word lists, syntactically structured nonword sentences and nonword lists. Neural activity in areas 6v and 55b contained speech- and language-related components, with stronger stimulus-condition effects in 55b, and stimulus condition was decodable in all three participants. In two larger datasets, semantic categories of English sentences were decodable from neural activity. These findings demonstrate that speech motor cortex encodes information about linguistic structure and semantic content at the level of sentences.

pending_articles.title: The Computational Grammar of Human Behaviour in a Biological Environment
pending_articles.content: Human behaviour unfolds as an extended stream of spontaneous actions shaped by environmental demands and the agent's goals. The organisation of these actions, situated between setting abstract goals and concrete movement execution, remains poorly characterised. Here, we introduce DynaClade, an unsupervised temporal action segmentation algorithm for human full-body motion capture data, and apply it to freely moving participants navigating ecologically realistic risky foraging environments in virtual reality. DynaClade identifies discrete actions whose kinematic characteristics and spatial distributions correspond to environmental affordances, supporting the validity of the approach. Among these actions, we discovered a hitherto undescribed movement pattern defined by increased body sway without locomotion. Action sequences were highly non-random and showed clear history dependence beyond first-order Markov structure, most of which was explained by a second-order prediction. This higher-order structure was well captured in a hidden Markov model, in which some of the observed actions were associated with more than one latent state. Each of these latent states corresponded to the same action in a distinct action context. These findings suggest that spontaneous human actions are predominantly selected based on the current action and context, rather than following pre-planned or habitually assembled sequences.

pending_articles.title: Loss of GluN2A Selectively Impairs Excitatory Synaptic Integration in Hippocampal Somatostatin Interneurons
pending_articles.content: N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) are widely considered key determinants of excitatory synaptic kinetics and activity-dependent plasticity, yet their specific contribution to postsynaptic potentials across distinct hippocampal CA1 cell types remains poorly defined. Null variants in GRIN2A are strongly associated with epilepsy-aphasia spectrum disorders, and GluN2A loss has recently been linked to delayed electrophysiological maturation of parvalbumin interneurons, a process regulated by somatostatin interneuron activity. Here, we used Grin2a haploinsufficient and knockout rats to determine how GluN2A depletion affects excitatory synaptic transmission, integration and firing across CA1 pyramidal neurons, parvalbumin interneurons and somatostatin interneurons. Using whole-cell patch-clamp recordings in acute hippocampal slices, we found that NMDARs made no discernible contribution to shaping Schaffer collateral-evoked EPSP kinetics, temporal summation or spike recruitment in CA1 pyramidal neurons at physiological resting potentials. Hebbian long-term potentiation at pyramidal neuron Schaffer collateral synapses was also preserved. Parvalbumin interneuron EPSP kinetics and synaptically evoked firing were similarly unaffected. By contrast, GluN2A loss selectively prolonged EPSP decay in CA1 somatostatin interneurons, increasing EPSP area, enhancing frequency-dependent temporal summation and elevating action potential output during repetitive and theta-frequency synaptic stimulation. These changes occurred alongside an increase in intrinsic excitability, indicating a cell-type-specific alteration by GluN2A loss. Selective enhancement of somatostatin interneuron recruitment provides a candidate mechanism - upstream of delayed parvalbumin interneuron maturation - and may contribute to hippocampal network dysfunction in GRIN2A-related disorders.
pending_articles.author: Hunter, D. W., Kaese, H., Kind, P. C., Wyllie, D. J.

pending_articles.title: Same Movements, Different Skills: How Context Shapes Learning in Humans and Neural Networks
pending_articles.content: What determines whether experiences are integrated into shared representations or split? Motor skill learning offers a revealing test: when two tasks require an identical sequence of movements, both intuition and theory suggest that practice in one should generalize to the other. Yet we find that changing context can make identical movements different skills. In simple recurrent networks trained on the same sequence across contexts, splitting was greatest when strong contextual inputs coincided with a high initial weight scale; neither alone sufficed. Greater representational separation coincided with separate context-specific learning curves. Humans practicing the same finger sequence while alternating between two performance-irrelevant contexts likewise exhibited context-specific curves, rather than the single continuous trajectory observed when practicing in a single context. State-space modeling favored split learning states in humans and very weakly coupled states in the most context-dependent networks. These findings have broader implications for understanding how learning generalizes across contexts.

When neuroscience meets machine learning: a taxonomic scoping review of machine and statistical learning approaches in sub-Saharan Africa
pending_articles.content: In high-resource economies, computational neuroscience research frequently employs machine learning (ML) and statistical learning (SL) techniques. While these methods provide effective ways to analyse multimodal, high-dimensional, and complex data they are underexplored in low resource settings. This taxonomic scoping review uses a systematic methodological approach to synthesise the application of ML and SL techniques in neuroscience research in sub-Saharan Africa. In addition to discussing findings, strengths, limitations, and future prospects, the work classifies current research by neuroscience domains, applications, learning tasks, datasets, tools, and techniques. In order for African researchers to contribute to and benefit from the global computational neuroscience landscape, our review contends that low- and middle-income countries must create and augment context-specific and representative datasets and incorporate appropriate features for model training. Future studies should focus on pragmatic rather than complex modelling, external validation, reproducibility, interpretability, and utilise real-world data to determine clinical utility.

recently_processed.title: Alpha-beta oscillatory dynamics underlying auditory inhibitory control in children
recently_processed.content: Response inhibition, the ability to withhold an unwanted response, is a fundamental component of cognitive control. While evoked responses in inhibitory tasks have been widely studied, induced oscillatory dynamics, particularly in the auditory modality and in children, remain largely unexplored. Here, we used magnetoencephalography (MEG) to examine induced alpha (8-12 Hz) and beta (13-20 Hz) oscillations during passive listening and an auditory Go/Nogo task in 67 children (6-14 years) and 16 adults (20-30 years). During passive listening, both groups showed an early alpha power increase in right fronto-temporo-parietal regions, followed by an alpha decrease in temporal regions. Under inhibitory demands, adults displayed a late alpha and beta power increase within a left fronto-temporo-occipital network, whereas children exhibited an early-onset, prolonged beta power decrease in somatomotor and temporo-parietal regions. Our findings indicate that children and adults engage spectrally, temporally, and spatially different neural dynamics during inhibitory control: in children, oscillatory modulation emerges earlier and is dominated by a beta decrease in sensorimotor regions, whereas adults recruit synchronized late alpha-beta dynamics in executive networks, possibly reflecting more efficient and evaluative inhibitory processing.
recently_processed.author: Finnilä, E., van Bijnen, S., Kujala, J., Parviainen, T.

recently_processed.title: How striatal neurons influence decision-making depends on broader circuit context: evidence from theory-driven cell type identification
recently_processed.content: Neural cell types are often conceived as having fixed computational roles, yet their behavioral contributions may depend on the broader circuit state. In the striatum, for example, direct and indirect pathway spiny projection neurons (SPNs) are typically described as facilitating or suppressing actions, respectively. However, emerging observations of striatal activity, such as modulation related to action timing, action vigor, and reactive inhibition, call this dichotomy into question. Here we develop a state-space framework linking striatal population activity to decision dynamics by combining a spiking cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic (CBGT) model with large-scale in vivo recordings from mice performing a two-choice task. Modeled activity patterns guided the inference of putative striatal SPN subtypes in the empirical recordings, enabling reconstruction of decision trajectories through an underlying state space. Across simulated and experimental data, these trajectories revealed a shared set of decision dynamics and identified three state-dependent roles of indirect pathway activity: preserving uncertainty when active alone, signifying choice commitment when coactive with the direct pathway in the same action channel, and slowing decisions when recruited in the opposing channel. To interpret these roles mechanistically, we mapped state transitions onto previously described basal ganglia control ensembles (responsiveness, pliancy, and choice) that translate circuit activity into the evidence accumulation process, and we found that each role was associated with a distinct pattern of control ensemble engagement that tunes decision policy. These analyses support a context-dependent view of SPN function, in which their moment-to-moment impact emerges from the evolving profile of dynamics throughout the CBGT circuit.

recently_processed.title: Postpartum resource scarcity reshapes maternal care, offspring prioritization, and the steroid-sensitive medial preoptic area
recently_processed.content: Parental care requires balancing offspring needs with environmental constraints, yet how resource scarcity alters the organization of maternal responses remains poorly understood. Here, we examined maternal behavior, offspring prioritization, and steroid receptor-associated extracellular matrix organization in postpartum rats exposed to limited bedding and nesting (LBN) or control conditions with ample nesting materials. LBN increased pup-directed and reduced self-directed behaviors but also increased behavioral entropy, a measure of behavioral fragmentation, indicating less predictable caregiving sequences. LBN dams preferentially retrieved male pups first, whereas control dams preferentially retrieved females first. LBN also increased the proportion of pup-investigation time directed toward males compared with controls. In offspring on postnatal day 10, corticosterone was elevated in female but not male LBN pups, a pattern that paralleled the maternal male bias. To identify associated neurobiological changes, we assessed steroid receptors and extracellular matrix organization in the medial preoptic area (mPOA), a key region for maternal behavior. LBN increased numbers of estrogen receptor  (ER)- and androgen receptor (AR)-immunoreactive cells, reduced perineuronal net (PNN) abundance, and decreased receptor-positive cell enwrapment. Because PNNs constrain structural plasticity, these findings suggest that the postpartum environment alters the organization of steroid receptor-associated extracellular matrix, potentially modulating experience-dependent plasticity in neurosteroid-sensitive circuits. In sum, LBN increases the levels of maternal engagement while reshaping its temporal organization and allocation, accompanied by selective remodeling of steroid-sensitive preoptic architecture. Therefore, maternal adaptation to adversity may be better understood as changes in caregiving allocation strategies rather than a simple gain or loss of maternal care.

recently_processed.title: Transcriptional and DNA Methylation Changes in the Hippocampus and Prefrontal Cortex after Fractionated Cranial Radiation in Mice
recently_processed.content: Fractionated whole-brain irradiation is essential for treating brain tumors, but many long-term survivors develop cognitive decline whose molecular basis is poorly understood. We asked which cell types and gene programs change late after irradiation, how the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex compare, and whether DNA methylation changes affect the same genes or programs. Male and female mice received whole-brain irradiation (5 x 4 Gy) or anesthesia alone. Irradiated mice showed persistent deficits in executive function and spatial memory. Eleven weeks after irradiation, single-nucleus RNA sequencing and whole-genome bisulfite sequencing of pooled hippocampal (CA1-3) and prefrontal tissue showed cell-type-specific transcriptional changes in neurons of both regions. Both regions showed reduced ribosomal-protein gene expression and changes in adhesion genes, with reduced respiratory-chain genes in prefrontal neurons and bidirectional synaptic gene changes in hippocampus. Differentially methylated regions were enriched at promoters, with hypermethylation predominating in three of the four sex-by-region contrasts. Methylation and gene expression changes pointed to overlapping synaptic and signaling programs, largely through different genes.

recently_processed.title: A common neural axis links image distinctiveness and memorability
recently_processed.content: Stimulus-specific memorability, the tendency for people to remember and forget the same stimuli, is a powerful predictor of memory performance that is independent of the study and retrieval factors that have dominated memory research. Critically, memorability can be defined in two ways: "Hit-ability" (H-ability) and "false alarm-ability" (FA-ability), the probability of correctly recognizing studied items or falsely recognizing unstudied items, respectively. Although past work has suggested that these are dissociable facets of memorability, challenging single-factor explanations, we present neural and computational evidence that they share a common neural axis. The neural signature of high H-ability matched the signature for low FA-ability, showing that these parameters have inverse relationships with a common factor. Moreover, we show that image distinctiveness predicts the flipped relationship between H-ability and FA-ability in both behavior and neural activity, providing a unifying explanation of stimulus-specific memorability.

recently_processed.title: Neuropathological assessment of cerebrovascular integrity in Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy
recently_processed.content: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy neuropathological change (CTE-NC) is defined by perivascular deposits of phosphorylated tau, with lesions preferentially located at sulcal depths. We investigated whether CTE-NC is associated with structural changes to perivascular spaces (PVSs) or microvascular degeneration. Post-mortem middle frontal gyrus tissue from 11 CTE-NC cases and 11 age-matched controls was examined using immunohistochemistry. All CTE-NC cases exhibited pathognomonic lesions in this region. We quantified PVS width along with vessel lumen and PVS area, string vessel burden, pericyte density, and aquaporin-4 (AQP4) polarisation to the astrocytic endfoot. Total PVS width did not differ significantly between the groups in grey matter (P = 0.543) nor white matter (P = 0.468). Neither PVS area (sulcal depth, P = 0.097; gyral crest, P = 0.645) nor PVS-to-lumen area ratio (sulcal depth, P = 0.454; gyral crest, P = 0.307) differed significantly. Similarly, there were no significant differences in total microvascular length (p = 0.693), string vessel burden (p = 0.128), pericyte density (p = 0.589), or AQP4 endfoot enrichment (p = 0.538). We therefore found no evidence of large-scale PVS enlargement, lumen narrowing, capillary degeneration, pericyte loss, or altered AQP4 endfoot enrichment in CTE-NC at the locations and spatial scales investigated. Taken together, these findings suggest that the pathognomonic perivascular tau lesion is not associated with a classical small vessel degenerative phenotype in CTE-NC. However, that does not exclude more subtle molecular, functional, or ultrastructural changes at the interface between vessels, the perivascular space, and surrounding brain tissue.
